triplets.head: Continental shelf doctrine (pre-1945)
triplets.tail: Sedentary fisheries near coast (pearl beds, sponge beds, oyster beds)

triplets.head: Continental shelf doctrine (pre-1945)
triplets.tail: No general doctrine of continental shelf existed

triplets.head: Continental shelf doctrine (pre-1945)
triplets.tail: 3 nautical miles

triplets.head: Emmerich de Vattel
triplets.tail: 18th-century Swiss jurist who justified coastal state appropriation of near-shore seabed resources as an appendage to the country they possess

triplets.head: Early sedentary fisheries claims
triplets.tail: Pearl beds of Ceylon/Bahrain, sponge beds off Tunisia, oyster beds off Ireland, pearl fisheries in Australia

triplets.head: Hall
triplets.relation: role in early continental shelf theory
triplets.tail: Recognized early claims on grounds of immemorial usage

triplets.head: Oppenheim
triplets.relation: role in early continental shelf theory
triplets.tail: Recognized early claims by treating seabed resources as products of land

triplets.head: Truman Proclamation
triplets.tail: Proclamation 2667

triplets.head: Truman Proclamation
triplets.tail: 28 September 1945

triplets.head: Truman Proclamation
triplets.tail: Geographic contiguity to coast; continental shelf as extension of the land-mass of the coastal nation

triplets.head: Truman Proclamation
triplets.tail: No depth or distance limit specified; relied on physical existence of the shelf

triplets.head: Truman Proclamation
triplets.tail: Natural resources of the subsoil and sea bed of the continental shelf subject to U.S. jurisdiction and control

triplets.head: Truman Proclamation
triplets.tail: Preserved high-seas status of waters above the shelf and free navigation

triplets.head: Truman Proclamation
triplets.tail: Boundaries with adjacent states to be determined by equitable principles

triplets.head: Truman Proclamation
triplets.tail: Triggered a cascade of similar claims globally

triplets.head: Harold L. Ickes
triplets.tail: Secretary of the Interior; prime mover who wrote June 1943 letter to Roosevelt advocating extension of U.S. jurisdiction

triplets.head: Harold L. Ickes
triplets.tail: Described shelf as extending 100–150 miles

triplets.head: Harold L. Ickes
triplets.tail: Pushed for unilateral approach

triplets.head: Breckinridge Long
triplets.tail: Assistant Secretary of State; co-chaired the Interdepartmental Study Group

triplets.head: Michael Straus
triplets.tail: Assistant Secretary of the Interior; co-chaired the Interdepartmental Study Group

triplets.head: Interdepartmental Study Group
triplets.tail: Interior, State, and Justice departments

triplets.head: Interdepartmental Study Group
triplets.tail: 13 July 1944

triplets.head: Joseph C. Grew
triplets.tail: Acting Secretary of State; signed January 1945 memorandum to President Roosevelt

triplets.head: Dean Acheson
triplets.tail: Acting Secretary of State; countersigned the Proclamation

triplets.head: State Department Office of Economic Affairs (ECA)
triplets.tail: Favored multilateral approach

triplets.head: State Department International Trade Policy (ITP) Division
triplets.tail: Favored multilateral approach

triplets.head: Santiago Declaration
triplets.tail: 18 August 1952

triplets.head: Santiago Declaration
triplets.tail: Chile, Ecuador, and Peru

triplets.head: Santiago Declaration
triplets.tail: Full sovereignty over seabed, subsoil, waters, and airspace to 200 nautical miles from coasts

triplets.head: Santiago Declaration
triplets.tail: Signatory countries lacked wide geological shelves but had rich fisheries; 200nm claim reflected economic/fisheries interests rather than geological features

triplets.head: Santiago Declaration
triplets.tail: Eventually had great impact on the development of the EEZ and continental shelf concepts

triplets.head: International Law Commission (ILC)
triplets.tail: Requested by the UN to codify customary international law of the oceans

triplets.head: J.P.A. François
triplets.tail: Special Rapporteur appointed in 1949 (Netherlands)

triplets.head: ILC 1951 Draft (3rd Session)
triplets.tail: Pure exploitability criterion — no fixed depth limit

triplets.head: ILC 1951 Draft (3rd Session)
triplets.tail: The sea-bed and subsoil of the submarine areas contiguous to the coast, but outside the area of territorial waters, where the depth of the superjacent waters admits of the exploitation of the natural resources of the sea-bed and subsoil

triplets.head: ILC 1951 Draft (3rd Session)
triplets.tail: Technical developments in the near future might make it possible to exploit resources of the sea-bed at a depth of over 200 metres

triplets.head: ILC 1951 Draft (3rd Session)
triplets.tail: Rights not based on customary law but on general principles of law

triplets.head: ILC 1951 Draft (3rd Session)
triplets.tail: Potentially unlimited outer boundary

triplets.head: J.P.A. François
triplets.tail: Favored flexible exploitability criterion

triplets.head: ILC 1953 Draft (5th Session)
triplets.tail: Fixed 200-metre depth limit, dropping the pure exploitability criterion

triplets.head: ILC 1953 Draft (5th Session)
triplets.tail: Response to widespread criticism that the 1951 definition lacked precision

triplets.head: ILC 1953 Draft (5th Session)
triplets.tail: Too rigid; disadvantaged some states without geological shelves

triplets.head: J.P.A. François
triplets.tail: Reversed course; proposed adding 200m depth limit for precision, arguing this was substituting a fixed limit for an indefinite one

triplets.head: Hersch Lauterpacht
triplets.tail: ILC member (UK); strongly supported 200m for legal certainty; argued without a fixed limit proposals would be valueless

triplets.head: J.M. Yepes
triplets.tail: ILC member (Colombia); opposed 200m; defended exploitability criterion as flexible and equitable; warned a depth-based definition would disadvantage Chile, Peru, and states without geological shelves

triplets.head: Hsu
triplets.tail: ILC member (China); supported François's 200m limit; questioned the term continental shelf as totally misleading

triplets.head: Kozhevnikov
triplets.tail: ILC member (USSR); proposed geological definition based on steep slope of seabed; criticized as impractical where no steep slope existed

triplets.head: Spiropoulos
triplets.tail: ILC member (Greece); noted no court could interpret the term steep slope — geographical, not legal term

triplets.head: Zourek
triplets.tail: ILC member (Czechoslovakia); noted 200m was somewhat arbitrary since geological declivity often at 400–500m

triplets.head: Sandstrom
triplets.tail: ILC member; raised concerns about limiting sovereign rights

triplets.head: ILC 1956 Draft (8th Session)
triplets.tail: Hybrid formula: fixed 200m depth baseline plus open-ended exploitability extension

triplets.head: ILC 1956 Draft (8th Session)
triplets.tail: Article 67

triplets.head: ILC 1956 Draft (8th Session)
triplets.tail: To a depth of 200 metres (approximately 100 fathoms) or, beyond that limit, to where the depth of the superjacent waters admits of the exploitation of the natural resources of the said areas

triplets.head: ILC 1956 Draft (8th Session)
triplets.tail: Exploitability criterion still open-ended

triplets.head: ILC 1956 Draft (8th Session)
triplets.tail: Continental shelf was now a legal fiction departing from geology

triplets.head: F.V. García Amador
triplets.tail: ILC member (Cuba); led the push to restore the exploitability criterion alongside the 200m limit at the ILC's 8th Session

triplets.head: J.P.A. François
triplets.tail: Opposed restoring exploitability criterion, fearing it would undermine stability of the 200m limit

triplets.head: Pal
triplets.tail: Opposed restoring exploitability criterion

triplets.head: ILC 1956 vote on exploitability clause
triplets.tail: Adopted 7 to 5

triplets.head: 1956 Inter-American Specialized Conference in Ciudad Trujillo
triplets.tail: Pushed back against pure 200m limit; Chile cited coal mining beyond 1,000m depth and 10–15 km offshore

triplets.head: 1958 Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf
triplets.tail: 26 April 1958 at UNCLOS I

triplets.head: 1958 Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf
triplets.tail: 10 June 1964

triplets.head: 1958 Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf
triplets.tail: Three criteria: adjacency, 200-metre depth, exploitability beyond 200m

triplets.head: 1958 Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf
triplets.tail: Adopted the ILC 1956 draft essentially unchanged

triplets.head: 1958 Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf
triplets.tail: Coastal states exercise exclusive sovereign rights for exploring and exploiting natural resources; rights exist ipso facto and ab initio

triplets.head: 1958 Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf
triplets.tail: Approximately 39 states

triplets.head: 1958 Geneva Convention on the Continental Shelf
triplets.tail: Exploitability criterion was open-ended — as technology advanced, claims could potentially extend to the entire ocean floor

triplets.head: ICJ North Sea Continental Shelf Cases
triplets.tail: 20 February 1969

triplets.head: ICJ North Sea Continental Shelf Cases
triplets.tail: Natural prolongation of land territory — geological concept, not depth or exploitability

triplets.head: ICJ North Sea Continental Shelf Cases
triplets.tail: Emphasized equitable principles over equidistance

triplets.head: ICJ North Sea Continental Shelf Cases
triplets.tail: Articles 1–3 of the 1958 Convention reflected received or at least emergent rules of customary international law

triplets.head: ICJ North Sea Continental Shelf Cases
triplets.tail: Directly set the stage for UNCLOS III

triplets.head: ICJ North Sea Continental Shelf Cases
triplets.tail: Undefined outer extent of natural prolongation

triplets.head: Judge Ammoun
triplets.tail: Judge from Lebanon; stated the first three articles of the Convention were intended to be broadly declaratory of existing customary international law

triplets.head: Judge ad hoc Sørensen
triplets.tail: Judge ad hoc for Denmark; summarized that the Convention's adoption was a very significant element in the process of creating new rules of international law

triplets.head: ICJ North Sea Continental Shelf Cases
triplets.tail: President José Bustamante y Rivero, Vladimir Koretsky, Gerald Fitzmaurice, Kōtarō Tanaka, Philip Jessup, Gaetano Morelli, Muhammad Zafrulla Khan, Luis Padilla Nervo, Isaac Forster, Andre Gros, Fouad Ammoun, César Bengzon, Sture Petrén, Manfred Lachs

triplets.head: ICJ North Sea Continental Shelf Cases
triplets.tail: Mosler (Germany), Max Sørensen (Netherlands)

triplets.head: Arvid Pardo
triplets.tail: Maltese Ambassador who proposed to the UN General Assembly in 1967 that the seabed beyond national jurisdiction be the common heritage of mankind

triplets.head: Arvid Pardo's 1967 speech
triplets.tail: Made the outer limit of the continental shelf simultaneously the inner limit of the international Area

triplets.head: Arvid Pardo's 1967 speech
triplets.tail: UN established the Committee on the Peaceful Uses of the Sea-Bed (Seabed Committee)

triplets.head: 1969 UNGA resolution
triplets.tail: Acknowledged that the 1958 Convention does not define with sufficient precision the limits of the continental shelf

triplets.head: 1969 UNGA resolution
triplets.tail: Led to convening of UNCLOS III in 1973

triplets.head: UNCLOS III
triplets.tail: 3 December 1973 in New York

triplets.head: UNCLOS III
triplets.tail: Nine years, 11 sessions

triplets.head: UNCLOS III
triplets.tail: 160+ states

triplets.head: UNCLOS III
triplets.tail: Consensus approach, package deal approach, single negotiating text (ISNT, ICNT)

triplets.head: UNCLOS III
triplets.tail: Second Committee

triplets.head: UNCLOS III
triplets.relation: dedicated group for continental shelf limits
triplets.tail: Negotiating Group No. 6 (NG6)

triplets.head: Broad-margin coastal states group (UNCLOS III)
triplets.tail: Argentina, Australia, Canada, Ireland

triplets.head: Broad-margin coastal states group (UNCLOS III)
triplets.tail: Wanted shelf to include slope and rise, extending to outer edge of margin

triplets.head: Superpowers group (UNCLOS III)
triplets.tail: United States and USSR

triplets.head: Superpowers group (UNCLOS III)
triplets.tail: Wanted a precise, clear definition

triplets.head: Landlocked/geographically disadvantaged states group (UNCLOS III)
triplets.tail: Demanded revenue-sharing beyond 200nm

triplets.head: Arab states and narrow-margin states group (UNCLOS III)
triplets.tail: Wanted shelf limited to 200nm

triplets.head: Hollis D. Hedberg
triplets.tail: American geologist/petroleum geologist who proposed the outer limit at a fixed distance (60 nautical miles) from the foot of the continental slope

triplets.head: Piers R.M. Gardiner
triplets.tail: Irish geologist who proposed the 1% sediment thickness formula in March 1976

triplets.head: Irish Amendments (1978)
triplets.tail: Circulated by the Irish delegation in the Second Committee of UNCLOS III

triplets.head: Irish Amendments (1978)
triplets.tail: Continental margin defined scientifically (shelf + slope + rise)

triplets.head: Irish Amendments (1978)
triplets.tail: Two formulae for outer edge: Gardiner (1% sediment) and modified Hedberg (60nm from FOS)

triplets.head: Irish Amendments (1978)
triplets.tail: Foot of slope = point of maximum change in gradient

triplets.head: Irish Amendments (1978)
triplets.tail: Method for fixing limits on charts using fixed points

triplets.head: Irish Amendments (1978)
triplets.tail: International boundary commission (became CLCS) as watchdog

triplets.head: Articles 76 and 82 of UNCLOS
triplets.tail: Package deal: broad-margin states accepted revenue-sharing obligations beyond 200nm (Art. 82) in exchange for extended shelf claims (Art. 76)

triplets.head: UNCLOS
triplets.tail: 30 April 1982

triplets.head: UNCLOS
triplets.tail: 130 in favour, 4 against, 36 abstentions

triplets.head: UNCLOS
triplets.tail: 10 December 1982 in Montego Bay

triplets.head: UNCLOS
triplets.tail: 16 November 1994

triplets.head: Article 76
triplets.tail: Within 200nm: purely juridical/distance-based; Beyond 200nm: scientific-legal hybrid

triplets.head: Article 76(1)
triplets.tail: Shelf extends to outer edge of continental margin, or 200nm from baselines, whichever is greater

triplets.head: Article 76(2)
triplets.tail: Shall not exceed limits provided in paragraphs 4–6

triplets.head: Article 76(3)
triplets.tail: Continental margin comprises shelf + slope + rise; excludes deep ocean floor and oceanic ridges

triplets.head: Article 76(4)(b)
triplets.tail: Foot of the continental slope is the point of maximum change in the gradient at its base

triplets.head: Foot of slope determination (general rule)
triplets.tail: Calculating the second derivative of bathymetric data to locate the point of maximum change in gradient

triplets.head: Foot of slope determination (general rule)
triplets.tail: Bathymetric data and digital elevation models (DEMs) derived from sonar surveys

triplets.head: Foot of slope determination
triplets.tail: When gradient-based method fails, geological and geophysical evidence can be used instead

triplets.head: Foot of slope (rifted margins)
triplets.tail: Landward limit of the continent-ocean transition (COT) zone may serve as the FOS (CLCS Guidelines 6.3.10)

triplets.head: Foot of slope (convergent margins)
triplets.tail: Seaward edge of the accretionary wedge or the foot of the inner trench wall/upper plate (CLCS Guidelines 6.3(a))

triplets.head: Article 76(4)(a)(i) — Gardiner/Irish Formula
triplets.tail: A line delineated by reference to the outermost fixed points at each of which the thickness of sedimentary rocks is at least 1 per cent of the shortest distance from such point to the foot of the continental slope

triplets.head: Article 76(4)(a)(i) — Gardiner/Irish Formula
triplets.tail: Sediment thickness relative to distance from foot of slope

triplets.head: Article 76(4)(a)(i) — Gardiner/Irish Formula
triplets.tail: Primarily seismic reflection profiling: sound waves transmitted into seabed, reflections from subsurface layers recorded

triplets.head: Article 76(4)(a)(i) — Gardiner/Irish Formula
triplets.tail: Two-way travel time of seismic wavelet converted to depth in meters using average velocity models; sediment thickness = vertical distance from seafloor to top of basement

triplets.head: Article 76(4)(a)(i) — Gardiner/Irish Formula
triplets.tail: (a) Produce contour maps of two-way travel time; (b) Produce contour maps of average velocities; (c) Convert travel times to depth maps using velocity distribution

triplets.head: Article 76(4)(a)(i) — Gardiner/Irish Formula
triplets.tail: Continental rises are composed of a wedge of sediment that thins seaward from the foot of the slope; 1% figure chosen so that coastal states would retain a significant part of the continental rise

triplets.head: Article 76(4)(a)(i) — Gardiner/Irish Formula
triplets.tail: Closely linked to criteria for evaluating presence of hydrocarbon resources — thicker sediment wedges associated with accumulation of organic-rich sediments that can generate oil and gas

triplets.head: Article 76(4)(a)(i) — Gardiner/Irish Formula
triplets.tail: Piers R.M. Gardiner (Irish geologist), March 1976

triplets.head: Article 76(4)(a)(ii) — Hedberg Formula
triplets.tail: A line delineated by reference to fixed points not more than 60 nautical miles from the foot of the continental slope

triplets.head: Article 76(4)(a)(ii) — Hedberg Formula
triplets.tail: Distance from the foot of the continental slope (geomorphological)

triplets.head: Article 76(4)(a)(ii) — Hedberg Formula
triplets.tail: Based on Hedberg's observation that the base of the continental slope is a remarkably distinctive and widespread feature but too broad and imprecise for a precise political boundary

triplets.head: Article 76(4)(a)(ii) — Hedberg Formula
triplets.tail: Allow for uncertainties in locating FOS; guarantee all coastal states receive entire submerged continental mass; provide uniform additional selvage; allow final boundary by simple straight lines

triplets.head: Article 76(4)(a)(ii) — Hedberg Formula
triplets.tail: Hollis D. Hedberg (American geologist)

triplets.head: Article 76(4)(a)(ii) — Hedberg Formula
triplets.tail: 100 km (~54nm); 60nm figure eventually adopted at UNCLOS III

triplets.head: Article 76 formulae application
triplets.tail: Coastal states may choose whichever formula is most favorable to them

triplets.head: Article 76 formulae
triplets.tail: Both formulae use the foot of the continental slope as their starting point/reference baseline

triplets.head: Article 76(5) — Constraint Line 1
triplets.tail: 350 nautical miles from baselines

triplets.head: Article 76(5) — Constraint Line 2
triplets.tail: 100 nautical miles seaward from the nearest point of the 2,500-metre depth contour (isobath)

triplets.head: Article 76(5) constraint lines
triplets.tail: Coastal state may use whichever constraint is more favorable (greater extent)

triplets.head: Article 76(6)
triplets.tail: On submarine ridges, the outer limit shall not exceed 350nm from baselines — the 2,500m isobath + 100nm constraint is NOT available

triplets.head: Article 76(6)
triplets.tail: Interpreted as synonymous with mid-ocean ridges (actively spreading plate boundary ridges traversing ~60,000 km of ocean)

triplets.head: Article 76(6)
triplets.tail: Introduced by Russia during UNCLOS III negotiations to prevent inordinate extension of claims along the mid-ocean ridge system

triplets.head: Article 76(6)
triplets.tail: Does not apply to submarine elevations that are natural components of the continental margin (plateaux, rises, caps, banks, spurs) — these remain subject to both paragraph 5 constraints

triplets.head: Article 76(6)
triplets.tail: Distinction between submarine ridges and submarine elevations is one of the most contested interpretive issues under Article 76

triplets.head: Article 76(7)
triplets.tail: Outer limits delineated by straight lines not exceeding 60 nautical miles in length, connecting fixed points defined by coordinates of latitude and longitude

triplets.head: Article 76(8)
triplets.tail: Submit data to CLCS; limits established on basis of CLCS recommendations are final and binding

triplets.head: Article 76(9)
triplets.tail: Charts and relevant information deposited with UN Secretary-General

triplets.head: Article 76(10)
triplets.tail: Does not prejudice delimitation between opposite/adjacent states

triplets.head: Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf (CLCS)
triplets.tail: Article 76(8) and Annex II of UNCLOS

triplets.head: CLCS
triplets.tail: 21 technical experts (geologists, geophysicists, hydrographers)

triplets.head: CLCS
triplets.tail: Elected by states parties, serving in personal capacities, 5-year renewable terms

triplets.head: CLCS
triplets.tail: Consider submissions and make recommendations

triplets.head: CLCS
triplets.tail: Provide scientific and technical advice

triplets.head: CLCS
triplets.tail: Submission → consideration by 7-member sub-commission → full CLCS recommendation (2/3 majority) → coastal state establishes limits → deposited with Secretary-General

triplets.head: CLCS
triplets.tail: After UNCLOS entered into force on 16 November 1994

triplets.head: Article 76 practical construction
triplets.tail: Determine the foot of slope (general rule: maximum gradient change; or evidence to the contrary)

triplets.head: Article 76 practical construction
triplets.tail: Apply two formulae: (a) FOS + 60nm (Hedberg); (b) FOS + 1% sediment thickness (Gardiner)

triplets.head: Article 76 practical construction
triplets.tail: Apply two constraints: (a) 350nm from baseline; (b) 2,500m isobath + 100nm

triplets.head: Article 76 practical construction
triplets.tail: On submarine ridges: only 350nm constraint available; on submarine elevations (natural components of margin): both constraints available

triplets.head: Article 76 practical construction
triplets.tail: Connect fixed points with straight lines not exceeding 60nm

triplets.head: 1994 Implementation Agreement
triplets.tail: Addressed Part XI (deep seabed mining) concerns of UNCLOS

triplets.head: ICJ Nicaragua v. Colombia (2012)
triplets.tail: Confirmed Article 76(1) reflects customary international law; declined to rule on paragraphs 2–9
